/- SamplingOptimisationGeometryBench public-dev reference.
   Reuses the existing project proof; retain LICENSE and NOTICE. -/
import AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Probability.RandomScanHeatBath
import AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Probability.KernelReversibility

open MeasureTheory ProbabilityTheory
open scoped ENNReal
open AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Probability
open AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Probability.RandomScanHeatBath
private theorem singleton_balance {n : ℕ} (μ : Measure (Fin (n + 1) → Bool))
    [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (x y : Fin (n + 1) → Bool) :
    μ {x} * randomScan μ x {y} = μ {y} * randomScan μ y {x} := by
  classical
  have hz (a b : Fin (n + 1) → Bool) (ha : μ {a} = 0) :
      μ {a} * randomScan μ a {b} = μ {b} * randomScan μ b {a} := by
    by_cases hb : μ {b} = 0
    · simp only [ha, hb, zero_mul]
    · rw [randomScan_apply_singleton μ b a hb]
      simp only [ha, zero_mul, mul_zero, ite_self, Finset.sum_const_zero]
  by_cases hx : μ {x} = 0
  · exact hz x y hx
  by_cases hy : μ {y} = 0
  · exact (hz y x hy).symm
  rw [randomScan_apply_singleton μ x y hx, randomScan_apply_singleton μ y x hy]
  simp only [← mul_assoc]
  rw [mul_comm (μ {x}) (n + 1 : ℝ≥0∞)⁻¹,
    mul_comm (μ {y}) (n + 1 : ℝ≥0∞)⁻¹, mul_assoc, mul_assoc]
  congr 1
  rw [Finset.mul_sum, Finset.mul_sum]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro i _
  have hsym : (∀ j, j ≠ i → y j = x j) ↔ (∀ j, j ≠ i → x j = y j) :=
    ⟨fun h j hj => (h j hj).symm, fun h j hj => (h j hj).symm⟩
  by_cases h : ∀ j, j ≠ i → y j = x j
  · have hf : (fun j => y (i.succAbove j)) = (fun j => x (i.succAbove j)) :=
      funext (fun j => h _ (Fin.succAbove_ne _ _))
    simp only [if_pos h, if_pos (hsym.mp h), hf]
    ac_rfl
  · simp only [if_neg h, if_neg (mt hsym.mpr h), mul_zero]

example {n : ℕ} (μ : Measure (Fin (n + 1) → Bool))
    [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] : Kernel.IsReversible (randomScan μ) μ :=
  KernelReversibility.isReversible_of_singleton_balance _ μ (singleton_balance μ)

For two supported atoms identifies symmetric site compatibility and equal fibers when compatible, then obtains the same weighted flux without changing the uniform averaging factor.

Tests/RandomScanHeatBathReversibility.lean checks the actual kernel including null starts and a disconnected two-bit target. Shares the existing public random-scan-null-atoms family; the complete balance-to-kernel proof is a different task from sogb-006's null-atom subproblem. No copied textbook wording or numbered exercise claim.
steps: Define \(J(x,y)=\mu(x)K(x,\{y\})\). If both atom masses vanish, both fluxes are zero. If \(\mu(x)=0<\mu(y)\), use the singleton formula at \(y\), never at \(x\). Each fiber \(F_i(y)\) contains \(y\) and therefore has positive mass; every allowed summand has numerator \(\mu(x)=0\). Thus \(K(y,\{x\})=0\) and \(J(x,y)=J(y,x)=0\). The case with \(x,y\) reversed follows by interchanging them.

If both masses are positive, each retained fiber of either start has positive mass. A site with \(x_{-i}\ne y_{-i}\) contributes zero to both fluxes. At a compatible site, \(F_i(x)=F_i(y)\), so the two unaveraged flux terms agree: \[\begin{aligned}\mu(x)q_i(x,y)&=\frac{\mu(x)\mu(y)}{\mu(F_i(x))}\\&=\mu(y)q_i(y,x).\end{aligned}\] Sum over the same sites with the same weight \(1/(n+1)\). This proves \(J(x,y)=J(y,x)\) for every pair, without dividing by a null mass.

On this finite space, expand the kernel on a set as the sum of singleton masses and the integral against \(\mu\) as a weighted sum. Then \[\begin{aligned}\int_A K(x,B)\,d\mu(x)&=\sum_{x\in A}\sum_{y\in B}J(x,y)\\&=\sum_{y\in B}\sum_{x\in A}J(y,x)\\&=\int_B K(y,A)\,d\mu(y).\end{aligned}\] The middle step uses atomic balance and reorders a finite sum. No irreducibility is needed.

Reversibility and \(K(x,X)=1\) give invariance by taking \(A=X\), not convergence from every start. For \(n=1\), give mass \(1/2\) to each of \(00,11\) and zero elsewhere. Each supported state is the only supported point in either of its retained fibers, so a single-site update leaves it fixed. Starting at \(00\) gives the same point mass at every time, distinct from \(\mu\). The two positive-mass states do not communicate.
